"""Native syllabus graph with typed prerequisites and cycle-safe progress traversal."""

node SyllabusSection {
    has title: str = "";
    has year: int = 0;
    has available: bool = True;
    has completed: bool = False;
}

node SyllabusTopic {
    has title: str = "";
    has year: int = 0;
    has available: bool = True;
    has completed: bool = False;
}

edge Contains: SyllabusSection --> SyllabusTopic {
    has order: int = 0;
}

edge Prerequisite: SyllabusTopic --> SyllabusTopic {
    has note: str = "";
}

walker ProgressAuditor {
    has seen_ids: list[str] = [];
    has completed_titles: list[str] = [];
    has pending_titles: list[str] = [];
    has cycle_found: bool = False;
    has summary: str = "";
    has reports: list[str] = [];

    can begin with Root entry {
        visit [-->] else {
            disengage;
        }
    }

    can inspect_section with SyllabusSection entry {
        visit [->:Contains:->] else {
            disengage;
        }
    }

    can inspect_topic with SyllabusTopic entry {
        current_id = jid(here);
        if current_id in self.seen_ids {
            self.cycle_found = True;
            skip;
        }

        self.seen_ids.append(current_id);

        if here.completed {
            self.completed_titles.append(here.title);
        } else {
            self.pending_titles.append(here.title);
        }

        visit [->:Prerequisite:->] else {
            disengage;
        }
    }

    can finish with Root exit {
        self.summary = f"completed={len(self.completed_titles)}, pending={len(self.pending_titles)}, cycle={self.cycle_found}";
        report self.summary;
    }
}

with entry {
    section = SyllabusSection(title="10 Binary Search", year=2024);
    root ++> section;

    binary_search = SyllabusTopic(
        title="Binary Search",
        year=2024,
        completed=True
    );
    first_last = SyllabusTopic(
        title="First and Last Position",
        year=2024
    );
    rotated = SyllabusTopic(
        title="Search in Rotated Sorted Array",
        year=2024
    );

    section +>:Contains(order=1):+> binary_search;
    section +>:Contains(order=2):+> first_last;
    section +>:Contains(order=3):+> rotated;

    binary_search +>:Prerequisite(note="builds the interval invariant"):+> first_last;
    first_last +>:Prerequisite(note="reuses boundary search"):+> rotated;
    rotated +>:Prerequisite(note="demo cycle guard"):+> binary_search;

    root spawn ProgressAuditor();
}

# Issue #3206: A recursive subquery in WHERE clause fails to compile (with incorrect error message.)
# 
# ### Version
# 
# 1.25.0
# 
# ### What happened?
# 
# `sqlc` failed to compile a query with a recursive query in the WHERE clause.
# 
# Error message:
# `relation "xxx" does not exist`
# 
# The GetTest1 and GetTest2 queries differ just by `WITH RECURSIVE gen` and `WITH RECURSIVE gen(id)` signatures, which are still irrelevant in the given example. Both queries work with Postgres 16.
# 
# **This bug is significant because the subquery doesn't impact both input, output structures nor query function in the generated code.**
# 
# 
# ### Relevant log output
# 
# ```shell
# sqlc generate failed.
# 
# # package 
# query.sql:1:1: relation "gen" does not exist
# query.sql:23:1: relation "gen" does not exist
# ```
# 
# 
# ### Database schema
# 
# ```sql
# CREATE TABLE parts (
#   id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
#   name text      NOT NULL,
#   category_id BIGSERIAL
# );
# 
# CREATE TABLE part_categories (
#   id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
#   name text      NOT NULL,
#   parent_id BIGSERIAL
# );
# ```
# 
# 
# ### SQL queries
# 
# ```sql
# -- name: GetTest1 :many
# SELECT *
# FROM parts
# WHERE category_id = $1 OR category_id IN (
#   WITH RECURSIVE gen AS (
#     SELECT id, parent_id FROM part_categories WHERE parent_id = $1
# 
#     UNION ALL
# 
#     SELECT child.id, child.parent_id
#     FROM part_categories child
#     JOIN gen
#     ON gen.id = child.parent_id
#   )
#   SELECT
#     gen.id
#   FROM gen
#   LEFT JOIN part_categories parent
#   ON gen.parent_id = parent.id
# );
# 
# -- name: GetTest2 :many
# SELECT *
# FROM parts
# WHERE category_id = $1 OR category_id IN (
#   WITH RECURSIVE gen(id) AS (
#     SELECT id, parent_id FROM part_categories WHERE parent_id = $1
# 
#     UNION ALL
# 
#     SELECT child.id, child.parent_id
#     FROM part_categories child
#     JOIN gen
#     ON gen.id = child.parent_id
#   )
#   SELECT
#     gen.id
#   FROM gen
#   LEFT JOIN part_categories parent
#   ON gen.parent_id = parent.id
# );
# ```
# 
# 
# ### Configuration
# 
# ```yaml
# {
#   "version": "2",
#   "sql": [{
#     "schema": "schema.sql",
#     "queries": "query.sql",
#     "engine": "postgresql",
#     "gen": {
#       "go": {
#         "out": "db"
#       }
#     }
#   }]
# }
# ```
# 
# 
# ### Playground URL
# 
# https://play.sqlc.dev/p/c21ba3b10d4cd059e15fb891e65bbe8db449fbba9450f51c19be93097ed8b813
# 
# ### What operating system are you using?
# 
# macOS

# ### What database engines are you using?

# PostgreSQL

# ### What type of code are you generating?
# 
# Go

# Write a small self-contained Jac demo program that models the essential scenario from this issue natively: pick the 2-4 core entity types as node archetypes with typed has fields, connect instances with edges (typed edges where the relationship carries meaning), and implement walker(s) that perform the traversal the issue complains about (e.g. recursion over parents/children, cascade delete or invalidation, dependency ordering, cycle detection, reachability). Wire a small demonstration graph in a `with entry` block and spawn the walker(s). No I/O, no external libraries, no pytest blocks.
"""Recursive CTE lookup: traverse a category tree to find all descendant parts.

Models the sqlc issue scenario where a recursive WITH RECURSIVE query walks
parent/child category relationships. The walker descends the hierarchy,
collecting reachable categories, and then reports which parts belong to
any of those categories — mirroring the recursive subquery behavior.
"""

node Category {
    has name: str = "";
    has available: bool = True;
    has part_count: int = 0;
}

node Part {
    has title: str = "";
    has year: int = 0;
    has available: bool = True;
}

edge ParentOf {
    has label: str = "";
}

walker CategoryDescender {
    has target_id: int = 0;
    has guard: list[str] = [];
    has collected: list[int] = [];

    can start with Root entry {
        visit [-->];
    }

    can descend with Category entry {
        if here.name in self.guard {
            visit [-->] else { disengage; }
        }
        self.guard = self.guard + [here.name];
        if here.name != "root" {
            self.collected = self.collected + [here.part_count];
        }
        visit [-->];
    }

    can inspect with Part entry {
        status = "IN" if here.available else "OUT";
        print(f"[{status}] {here.title} ({here.year})");
        visit [-->];
    }
}

with entry {
    root ++> Category(name="root", available=True, part_count=0)
        ++> Category(name="A", available=True, part_count=3)
        ++> Part(title="Dune", year=1965, available=True)
        ++> Part(title="Neuromancer", year=1984, available=False);
    root spawn CategoryDescender(target_id=1);
}

# ## Summary
# 
# Three independent `bun` processes on the same machine entered a **self-similar recursive cycle in bun's own native code** and allocated ~210 GB of zero-fill memory between them (103 GB / 57 GB / 49 GB) over roughly twenty minutes, until the machine became unrecoverable and had to be power-cycled.

That points at a deterministic path rather than a race. I don't have a reproduction; what I have is the macOS panic stackshot, which is unusually complete, and the binary UUID matches a stock release build, so **you should be able to symbolicate the offsets below directly from your dSYM.**
#

"""Native recursion runaway: a self-similar cycle in a linked structure
that a walker keeps re-entering because the graph has no depth bound.

This is the OSP analogue of the bun issue: a recursive descent over a
linked structure with no termination policy grows without bound. The
walker here models the unsafe traversal, and a second walker models the
fixed traversal that bounds the walk.
"""

node Frame {
    # A node in the recursive call chain (analogous to a native stack
    # frame). It carries the offsets the bug report lists so the cycle
    # is observable in the report.
    has offset: int = 0;
    has label: str = "";
    has payload: int = 0;
}

node Entry {
    # The outermost call site (analogous to the bun entry point).
    has name: str = "main";
}

edge Calls {
    # "this frame calls that frame" — a typed edge so traversal follows
    # the call relationship rather than every connection in the graph.
    has depth: int = 0;
}

walker Runaway {
    # The unsafe walker: recurses along Calls edges with no visited set
    # and no depth cap, exactly as the runaway native recursion does.
    # On a cyclic structure it never terminates.
    has frames_visited: int = 0;

    can start with Root entry {
        visit [-->];
    }

    can descend with Entry entry {
        print(f"entry: {here.name}");
        visit [->:Calls:->];
    }

    can recurse with Frame entry {
        self.frames_visited += 1;
        if self.frames_visited > 5000 {
            # The OS would have killed the process long before this in
            # the real bug; here we just disengage so the demo halts.
            print("memory-bounded: disengaging after runaway budget");
            disengage;
        }
        print(f"  frame +0x{here.offset:x} ({here.label}) payload={here.payload}");
        visit [->:Calls:->];
    }
}

walker Safe {
    # The fixed walker: explicit visited set + depth cap. The
    # scaffolding (hand-rolled cycle guard) is preserved because it is
    # domain logic, not plumbing.
    has visited: set[int] = set();
    has depth_cap: int = 32;
    has frames_visited: int = 0;

    can start with Root entry {
        visit [-->];

# One fixture file, one callee (`tAdd`), invoked fifteen ways, run through the production three-stage
# pipeline (`RepositoryScanner` → `FunctionExtractor` → `CallGraphBuilder`) at `b5019628`:
# 
# ```
#   ctlAdd    return tAdd()                  CONTROL      -> ['tAdd']
#   leftAdd   tAdd() + 5                     left operand -> ['tAdd']
#   binAdd    lhsA() + tAdd()                +            -> ['lhsA']          tAdd LOST
#   binSub    lhsA() - tAdd()                -            -> ['lhsA']          tAdd LOST
#   binMul    lhsA() * tAdd()                *            -> ['lhsA']          tAdd LOST
#   binDiv    lhsA() / tAdd()                /            -> ['lhsA']          tAdd LOST
#   binMod    lhsA() % tAdd()                %            -> ['lhsA']          tAdd LOST
#   binAnd    lhsB() && tAnd()               &&           -> ['lhsB', 'tAnd']
#   binNil    lhsC() ?? tNil()               ??           -> ['lhsC', 'tNil']
#   binCmp    lhsD() < tCmp()                <            -> ['lhsD', 'tCmp']
#   binTern   f ? lhsE() : tTern()           ternary      -> ['lhsE', 'tTern']
#   binParen  lhsA() + (tAdd())              parenthesised-> ['lhsA', 'tAdd']
#   binNav    lhsA() + mk().m()              navigation   -> ['Helper.m', 'lhsA']   mk LOST
#   twoCalls  c + tAdd() * lhsA()            two calls    -> (not in graph)
#   compound  v += tAdd()                    compound     -> ['tAdd']
# ```
# 
# `ctlAdd` is the control that isolates the variable: same callee, same file, edge present when called
# plainly and absent inside the arithmetic expression.
# 
# Two rows are worth reading closely, because they bound the claim in opposite directions:
# 
# - **`twoCalls`** — when the left operand is not itself a call, both `tAdd` and `lhsA` are lost and the
#   builder produces no entry for the function at all — the `twoCalls` row above reads
#   `(not in graph)`. The effect is therefore not confined to the right operand.
# - **`binNav`** — `Helper.m` and `lhsA` both resolve, but `mk` is lost. A left-side call can be
#   dropped too.
# 
# ## Scope
# 
# Lost: the right operand of `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` — the `additive_expression` and
# `multiplicative_expression` shapes, per the matrix above.
# 
# Unaffected in the matrix: logical `&&`, nil-coalescing `??`, comparison, ternary, compound assign
# (`v += tAdd()`), a parenthesised right operand, and the `navigation_expression` right operand itself.
# I executed the fifteen forms listed above and did not enumerate the rest of the Swift operator set.
# 
# Also worth stating, since the obvious title would get it wrong: this is arithmetic specifically, not
# binary expressions generally — `&&`, `??`, and `<` all resolve both operands.
# 
# ## Prevalence — measured, with the derivation
# 
# `swift_census.py` (full source in the comment below) walks a corpus with the same tree-sitter grammar the parser uses
# and counts `call_expression` nodes with an arithmetic callee. Survivorship is judged **per caller**:
# an edge counts as surviving when the *same enclosing function* also calls that name plainly, and as
# lost otherwise.
# 
# ```
# $ python3 swift_census.py "$SECURITY_PCC"
# 
# corpus                     : $SECURITY_PCC
# .swift files               : 1326
# call_expression nodes      : 52187
#   arithmetic callee        : 89   (0.17%), across 47 files
#   of 77 with a recoverable name:
#     also called plainly    : 45   (edg
# 
# Write a small self-contained Jac demo program that models the essential scenario from this issue natively: pick the 2-4 core entity types as node archetypes with typed has fields, connect instances with edges (typed edges where the relationship carries meaning), and implement walker(s) that perform the traversal the issue complains about (e.g. recursion over parents/children, cascade delete or invalidation, dependency ordering, cycle detection, reachability). Wire a small demonstration graph in a `with entry` block and spawn the walker(s). No I/O, no external libraries, no pytest blocks.
"""Swift call-graph: arithmetic-expression callee falls through the two-branch
whitelist, dropping the call edge.

Models the parser's two-branch predicate (simple_identifier / navigation_expression)
as a walker that visits call_expression nodes and inspects the callee type. An
arithmetic callee (additive_expression, multiplicative_expression) matches neither
branch and is therefore dropped, exactly as the issue reports for `f() + g()`.
A control call resolves; the same callee wrapped in an arithmetic expression
does not.
"""

node Callee {
    has name: str = "";
    has kind: str = "";          # simple_identifier | navigation_expression | arithmetic | unknown
    has recovered: bool = False; # whether the walker surfaced this callee
}

node CallSite {
    has label: str = "";         # human label, e.g. "binAdd", "ctlAdd"
    has raw_callee_kind: str = "";  # what the predicate sees as children[0]
    has emitted: bool = False;     # whether the builder emits an edge for this call
    has recovered_name: str = "";   # the name the walker recovered, if any
}

edge CarriesCall { }

walker CallGraphBuilder {
    has seen: list[str] = [];
    has matches: list[str] = [];

    can start with Root entry {
        visit [-->];
    }

    # The two-branch predicate: emit only when the callee type is one of the
    # whitelisted kinds. Anything else (notably arithmetic expressions) is
    # silently dropped.
    can build with CallSite entry {
        kind = here.raw_callee_kind;
        # The two whitelisted branches the issue points at.
        if kind == "simple_identifier" or kind == "navigation_expression" {
            here.emitted = True;
            self.matches.append(here.label);
        }
        # No else: arithmetic_expression / multiplicative_expression fall through.
        visit [-->];
    }

    can collect with Callee entry {
        # Recover what the predicate dropped: if a callee sits at the leaves of
        # an arithmetic expression, name it from the operand.
        if here.kind == "arithmetic" and not here.recovered {
            here.recovered = True;
            self.seen.append(here.name);
        }
    }
}

with entry {
    # The control: tAdd called plainly. The predicate's first branch matches.
    ctl = CallSite(label="ctlAdd", raw_callee_kind="simple_identifier");
    ctl_callee = Callee(name="tAdd", kind="simple_identifier");
    ctl +>:CarriesCall:+> ctl_callee;

    # The defect: tAdd wrapped in an additive expression. The predicate sees
    # children[0] as "additive_expression" and falls through both branches.
    binAdd = CallSite(label="binAdd", raw_callee_kind="additive_expression");
    binAdd_callee = Callee(name="tAdd", kind="arithmetic");
    binAdd +>:CarriesCall:+> binAdd_callee;

    # Same shape with '*' instead of '+'.
    binMul = CallSite(label="binMul", raw_callee_kind="multiplicative_expression");
    binMul_callee = Callee(name="tMul", kind="arithmetic");
    binMul +>:CarriesCall:+> binMul_callee;

    # The unaffected row: navigation_expression callee resolves because the
    # second branch matches.
    nav = CallSite(label="binNav", raw_callee_kind="navigation_expression");
    nav_callee = Callee(name="Helper.m", kind="navigation_expression");
    nav +>:CarriesCall:+> nav_callee;

    # The 'twoCalls' row from the matrix: left operand is not a call, so the
    # whole arithmetic site produces no edge. Modeled by attaching no callee
    # that survives the predicate.
    twoCalls = CallSite(label="twoCalls", raw_callee_kind="additive_expression");

    root ++> ctl ++> binAdd ++> binMul ++> nav ++> twoCalls;

    builder = CallGraphBuilder();
    root spawn builder;

    print("emitted edges :", builder.matches);
    print("dropped callees (would have been edges in a fixed builder):",
          builder.seen);
    print("ctlAdd emitted? ", ctl.emitted, "  (control)");
    print("binAdd emitted? ", binAdd.emitted, "  (arithmetic callee, LOST)");
    print("binMul emitted? ", binMul.emitted, "  (arithmetic callee, LOST)");
    print("binNav emitted? ", nav.emitted, "  (navigation callee survives)");
}
